ARINC 429 DATA BUS
OBJECTIVES
w Describe and interpret different message formats.
w Describe and interpret different word formats.
w Identify basic principles of operation related to the ARINC 429 data bus system specifications.
w Describe the ARINC 429 Mark 33 Digital Information Transfer System (DITS).
EQUIPMENT REQUIRED

This lesson describes ARINC specification 429 known as the Mark 33 Digital Information Transfer System (DITS). This system is commonly called ARINC 429 DITS, and is referred to as ARINC 429 DITS throughout this lesson.
INTRODUCTIONM
You will be introduced to the basic operating principles, message formats, and word structures covered by the specification.
This specification became necessary as the complexity of today's modern aircraft systems increased. This increase demanded a reliable, maintainable, and standard method of data transfer.
A standard method of data transfer is necessary to enable communication between system components made by different manufacturers.
The standard also enables system designers to develop new equipment that is compatible with existing systems.

Equipment made from different manufacturers designed for the ARINC 429 DITS specification should be interchangeable or Line Replaceable Units (LRUs). This allows a failed piece of equipment to be easily replaced with an entirely new piece.

LESSON MENU
OPERATING PRINCIPLES

The ARINC 429 DITS specifies the data transfer procedures between avionics system elements. This data transfer is accomplished through a single twisted pair of shielded wires. Communication is uni-directional and simplex.
DISCUSSION
One avionics system element can transmit data over the bus to no more than 20 receiving system elements that require information. Bi-directional data transfer is not permitted.

The shields are grounded at both ends to an aircraft ground which is close to the rack connector and at all production breaks in the cable. Grounding is necessary to reduce undesired error in the system data transfer.
Unlike some data transfer systems, the ARINC 429 DITS does not use bus controllers, remote transmitters or bus monitors to control data flow.

The ARINC 429 DITS transfers data through the twisted wire pair using a tri-level signal. The signal can be either HI, NULL or LOW. This data is transferred at one of two data speed rates, HIGH or LOW.
High speed data transfer, 100 kbps, is used to send large amounts of data or flight critical information. Flight critical information for example could be communication with the auto pilot.
Low speed data transfer, 12 to 14.5 kbps, is used for non-critical or general purpose applications. Non-critical information for example could be communications with a radio.

The ARINC 429 DITS as stated earlier transfers data through the twisted wire pair using a tri-level signal. This signal, after sending a bit of data, returns to null before sending the next bit. This is known as "Return to zero modulation."
Similar to the RS-485 bus, the ARINC 429 DITS uses a balanced differential bus. Remember that a balanced differential bus takes the difference of two signals to produce a virtually noise free output.

These output signals from the transmitter should have the voltage levels specified in the chart below for each of the three output states. Note that these levels are measured when the transmitter circuit is open and balanced to ground.

The input signals to the receiver should have the voltage levels specified in the chart below. Note the range is large enough to account for a wide range of voltage levels. This is necessary due to the different operating conditions of different systems.

When input signals to the receiver are not within the specified values the receiver should discontinue operation. However, this is not an ARINC 429 DITS specification and will be dependent on the manufacturer of the receiver.

Another important specification of ARINC 429 DITS is the transmitter output impedance. The output impedance should be about 75 ohms equally divided between line A and B, providing an impedance balanced output. This impedance value should be present during all three states of the output.
The receiver impedance values should be as listed below. Note that the specification includes both resistance and capacitance values.

Standard voltage levels and impedance values are important for system compatibility. Without these standards, different system components may not be compatible making system design and troubleshooting difficult.

Receivers should be designed to withstand faulted system conditions. If a receiver may possibly cause loss of data to other receivers it should isolate itself from the system. This allows a system to communicate with other receivers if one becomes faulty, instead of faulting the entire system.
A transmitter should withstand the following faulted system conditions without damage: short circuits from line A to B, line A to ground, line B to ground, and line A to B to ground.
A receiver should withstand the following faulted system conditions without damage: 30 VAC across line A and B, 29 VDC across line A and ground, or 29 VDC across line B and ground.

While protection for every possible fault is not necessary, these specifications provide protection for the most probable and critical faults. Protecting against every possible fault would make systems more expensive, take up more space and add additional weight to the aircraft.

The ARINC 429 DITS uses two types of data transfer protocol. Old systems may use the character-oriented protocol, while new systems use the bit-oriented protocol. The bit-oriented protocol has become the ARINC 429 DITS standard.
A bit-oriented system can use both bit and character oriented protocol, while character-oriented systems can only use character-oriented protocol to support older equipment connected to the system.
The ARINC 429 DITS uses five basic 32-bit word formats to send data. These different word formats are: BCD, BNR, discretes, acknowledgments and alphanumeric.

Spare labels are also provided in the event that expansion becomes necessary. The ARINC 429 DITS word formats will be discussed in the next objective, ARINC 429 DITS Protocol.

Finally, while the ARINC 429 DITS is uni-directional, bi-directional communication can be established with additional components and twisted pair bus wires. For modern civil aircraft this is acceptable, but for military aircraft the MIL-STD-1553 DITS would be used instead.

ARINC 429 DITS PROTOCOL

There are currently six different types of data used to transmit information. Each of these data types can be encoded in a multiple number of word formats. Remember, a word is the information transmitted on the bus.
DISCUSSION

Different data types can use the same word format, the information they transmit is the difference. Word formats provide a shell in which data can be encoded by a transmitter and understood by other equipment. All words used on the ARINC 429 DITS are 32-bits long.

All of the word formats provide at least identification and error checking. All other information contained within a particular format is dependent on the application. Let's look at each of the data types and their respective word formats.

There are two word formats associated with numeric data; BCD and BNR. The first one we will look at is BCD or Binary Coded Decimal. The numeric BCD word format is used to encode data on things like: setting latitude, setting longitude, or estimated time of arrival, just to name a few.
The example shown below is a Numeric BCD word. Let's look at each part of the word to understand its relationship to the word format and to the ARINC 429 system.

The first 8 bits of the word are known as the label. The label indicates what type of information is about to follow. Used along with the label is the equipment code (it is not actually contained within the word).

The 8 bits of the label are broken down into three octal numbers. Notice that one of the numbers only has two bits, this number can only go to three. The range for the label is 000 to 377 octal. In our example the label 00001101 corresponds to 260. Notice that bit 1 is the MSB (Most Significant Bit) and bit 9 is the LSB (Least Significant Bit).

After identifying the label, the word and its information can be found on the label table. The equipment code is 031 hex. Below is a small section of a label table with our label highlighted. Our information will contain a date, but not a flight leg.

Notice that if the equipment code was 0A2 we would know that the following data would also contain the flight leg. If the equipment code was 02C the data would be about fuel quantity and unrelated to date (031). This is why the equipment code is very important.

The next two bits of the word are known as the SDI, or Source/Destination Identifier. While in most applications the functions of these bits are not used, they will still be covered in this lesson. Also note, if the functions of SDI are not used these bits should be set to 0.

The SDI can provide one of two features, either identify equipment as a transmitter (source), receiver (sink), or both, or distinguish between equipment in multi-system applications. The details of these features will not be explained, but the binary settings and meanings are listed below.

The next 19 bits of the word are the data. Data is encoded and placed within the word starting from the left (MSB). All bits that are not used for data are filled with 0s, this is known as padding. Discrete data, which will be covered later, can be filled into the padded bits starting from the right (LSB).

While each part of the data will be encoded with BCD, the actual structure of the data is dependent on the application. In our example word you cannot determine how the date is encoded without looking at a diagram showing you the format. The format for our date is shown below.

The next two bits of the word are known as the SSM or Sign/Status Matrix. The first function of the SSM is to indicate the sign of data; positive, negative, north, below, etc. The actual sign being indicated is dependent on the data.
1 1 Minus, South, West, Left, From, Belowww
1 1 Minus, South, West, Left, From, Below

The second function of the SSM is to indicate the receiving equipment if there is no computed data (for reasons other than a functional failure). The last function of the SSM is to instruct the receiving equipment to perform a functional test. Note that only one of these three functions can be sent in a single word.

If the sign function is not being used than these bits should be padded until either of the two other functions are needed. In our example word the use of the sign function isn't needed so the spaces are padded with 0s.

The last bit of the word is the parity bit. ARINC 429 uses odd parity for error checking, meaning the total number of high data bits plus the parity bit equals an odd number. In our example there is 7 high bits in the data field. The parity bit must be set to 0 for the total of both to be odd.

If the received word contained 8 high bits in the data field and zero for the parity bit, you would know the data was invalid. However, if two data bits are wrong then the number will still be odd and the receiver will think the information is valid.

The second difference between the BCD and BNR word formats is the SSM or Sign/Status Matrix. Instead of two bits, the BNR SSM contains three bits. By using this third bit the sign matrix and status matrix functions have been separated.

The sign matrix is bit 29. A 0 will indicate: plus, north, east, right, to and above. A 1 will indicate: minus, south, west, from and below. From our example we can see that the velocity is in the north direction.

In our example word the status matrix is set to 11 indicating that operation is normal. If the status matrix had shown 00 the data retrieved from the word may not be correct. These additional status messages allow more control and monitoring of the ARINC 429 data being transferred.

The last bit of the word, bit 32, is the parity bit. Again, the parity bit added to the data bits should equal an odd number. Our example word has three high data bits so the parity bit must be set to 0 for the final total to remain an odd number.

Definition

This type of data pertains to information, performance, operation and maintenance. Discrete data is separated into 2 groups; general purpose and dedicated. Let's look at general purpose discrete data.

General purpose discrete data follows one simple format, the discrete word format. This format is almost identical to the BCD word format, the only difference being the data field. The example word below will be used to explain the components of the discrete data word.
P SSM DISCRETE DATA SDI LABELLLLLLLLLLLLL

As with the BCD format, the first 8 bits of the discrete word are used for the label. The label will indicate one of two types of general purpose discrete data: flight control or maintenance. Flight control labels are from 145 to 147 and from 270 to 276. Maintenance labels are from 155 to 161 and 350 to 354.

The label to our example word indicates 271, and we will use the equipment code 033. This information indicates that the information following the label is flight control data. Maintenance discrete data will be covered later under maintenance data.

The next step would be to look up this label type in a label table to determine what the information represents. The SDI, SSM and Parity bit fields will not be discussed since their operation is identical to that of the BCD word format. The table below illustrates the functions of each data bit.

ALPHANUMERIC DATA

The next data type we will examine is alphanumeric data. Alphanumeric data is split in two categories; message data and maintenance data. This word format is used when the transfer of text is required.
Message data has four word formats; initial, control, intermediate, and final. The example below illustrates the text "Nida Corporation". The first word we will look at is the initial word.
The label of the initial word will be either 356 or 357. 356 corresponds to message data, and 357 corresponds to maintenance data. Note that all four word types will use the same label. . G

The next field of data in the initial word is the word count, bits 9 through 16. This value is encoded in binary with a maximum value of 255. This number should represent the number of words that will follow the initial word. In our example the binary value indicates that 6 words will follow.

The next 6 bits, 17 through 22, are padded with zeros. Bits 23 through 29 contain the ISO Alphabet #5 character "STX". The ISO alphabet #5 is the standard method for encoding text for transfer in the ARINC 429 DITS protocol.

The next word to follow is optional and not contained in our example words. This word is known as the control word. The control word is used when messages are used to drive displays. The control word contains information like; the number of lines, color, intensity, character size and a command to make the message flash.

The control word also uses the same label used by the initial word. The SSM value for the control word is 11 which can be seen in the chart below. The encoding methods for the control word will not be discussed in this lesson.

The next word used for alphanumeric data is the intermediate word. The intermediate word is used to transmit three characters at a time for all but the last few characters. Notice that our example word contains 5 intermediate words.

The label for all intermediate words should be identical to the initial word label. The next 21 bits of the word are used to encode three ISO Alphabet #5 characters. If a space is not to have a character it should contain all 0s.

In our example word we can see that the first character, bits 9 through 15, correspond to the character "N". The second two characters "i" and "d". Notice that the SSM field is set to 00, indicating that it is an intermediate word.

The last word of the sequence, the final word, is formatted almost identically to the intermediate word, the only difference being the SSM field, which in the final word is set to 10. All unused characters in the final word are padded (filled with 0s). The label of the final word should also be identical to that of the initial word, 357.

By decoding all of the characters in our sample word sequence we can see that the text data being sent was "Nida Corporation". Notice that two character locations of the last bit were padded with 0s since there was no more characters to send.

A new type of data which may eventually be used on the ARINC 429 DITS is graphic data. Graphics data includes; lines, circles, symbols, and randomly positioned text. A format has not been established for graphic encoding.
This type of data transfer is used when large amounts of data need to be sent, for example a flight plan information upload.

There are two methods for file transfer; bit-oriented protocol and and character-oriented protocol. All equipment that uses bit-oriented protocol can use character-oriented, however, older equipment normally uses character-oriented protocol only.
It was determined that a universal method of data transfer was needed for compatibility between different systems. The bit-oriented protocol became the standard.
Character-oriented protocol is not much different than the alphanumeric formats. The bit-oriented protocol, on the other hand, is very much different.

Remember, the old standard was character-oriented protocol until a universal transfer method was needed. This is when the bit-oriented protocol became the file transfer data standard.

1. These are the five basic types of data transfer used on the ARINC 429 DITS.
2. There are two methods used in encoding numeric data; BCD (Binary Coded Decimal) and BNR (Straight Binary). The straight binary is encoded in two's complement fractional notation.
3. Discrete data is either general purpose or dedicated. General purpose discrete data uses the discrete word format while dedicated discrete data is placed in the padded bits of another word.

4. Alphanumeric data is split into two types; message and maintenance dat. There are four word formats that are associated with the alphanumeric data. These word types are initial, control, intermediate and final.

5. Maintenance data is split into two types; general and acknowledgment. General maintenance data is encoded using word formats from numeric data, discrete data and even alphanumeric data. The acknowledgment maintenance data format has not completely been determined yet.

6. The need for graphic data transfer on the ARINC 429 DITS is becoming necessary. Ideas have been established but actual word to transfer bit-oriented data assembled in data files formats are still to be determined.

7. There are two different methods for file transfer; bit-oriented protocol and character-oriented protocol. The bit-oriented protocol has become the standard for data transfer. All equipment that will transfer bit-oriented data will also transfer character-oriented data, however, most older systems only transfer character-oriented data.
